and it remains at 7 cents afterwards. But when a man is promoted to the rank of corporal he loses his good conduct pay, for what reason no one has ever been able to say. But it is another mysterious question one would like to have answered or solved in some way.
Men at present are buying their discharges thoroughly disgusted at the treatment they are receiving. Some of the permanent force depots are 30 or more under strength and no signs of any amelioration in the present state of affairs. Certainly with plenty of work outside and good wages one cannot be expected to work for 40 cents per day.
These are a few points when the Bill comes up again, Sir. Another thing the Bill says, which I notice the pay is only as regards ' pri-Mr. INGRAM.
vates,' nothing about the non-commissioned officers' pay. They presume to settle it by an Order in Council, hut pay for all ranks should be settled by the House itself, which should be the supreme power in dealing with this most Important question.
I must apologize to the House for having lead this document, but it puts the facts better than I could state them.

The House will see how impossible it would be to set forth in an Act all the intricate details referred to in the letter which the hon. gentleman has read. The concluding portion of ihe letter referred to the pay of the private, which is now 40 cents per day. Well, we are increasing it to 75 cents. Three or four years ago the permanent force had no provision made for pensions, but to-day there is a pension provided for the man who has served twenty years. Of course, the pay of the noncommissioned officer will be increased relatively or to a greater extent than that of the privates. The non-commissioned officers are being treated exactly as the officers. The Governor General in Council will fix their pay just as the King's regulations fix the pay in the British army. I think the sergeants will fare better in the way I propose than to have the amount paid them tied up by Act of parliament. Times are changing and wages are increasing and it is desirable that as much elasticity as possible should be left to the department in dealing with matters of this kind. My own first idea was to leave the whole pay to the Governor in Council, as is done in Austi'alia. but on second thought I deemed it wise to fix the rate of pay for privates by Act of parliament. The whole desire of the officers in command of the militia is to reward good men, and none of those non-commissioned officers who are zealous and anxious to do their duty need be afraid that they will not be fairly treated under the provisions we propose.

In view of its being difficult to get men, I thought that by doing away with the system by Order in Council the men might receive more pay than if it were fixed by Act of parliament. I would like to draw the attention of the hon. minister to the fact that to-day it is difficult in many cases to get men to do anything. They are either scarce or require very high pay. If that is a difficulty outside, how much more difficult must it be for the department to secure good men for very low pay. As I understand it now, the minister has not given a definite answer, but has said he will consider the matter, and when the Bill is before the House he may change his views.

I shall be glad to consider it. One word more with reference to pay. "While it is quite true that it is more difficult for the government to get

men, it is not desirable that the government should compete with the regular industries of the country. I shall read the letters in ' Hansard. '
Hon. Win. BOSS (Victoria, N.S.) There should be some distinction between those who have served a year or two in camp and those who go into camp for the first time. The Prime Minister has quoted the case of the man who came in at the eleventh hour and got the same wages as the one who had worked all day, but that caused great dissatisfaction in the ranks. They were not pleased with the Master. The same-thing will happen here. Unless you give the men who have served two years somewhat better pay than the green hands, there will be dissatisfaction in the ranks.
Respecting the pay of the district officers commanding, is there any provision made to increase it 1
Later on that is dealt with.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I would suggest that an amendment be made by striking out all the words after the word ' allowances ' in the second resolution and inserting the following
Shall be at the rate of 50 cents a day, which rate may be increased as may be prescribed by regulation to be approved by the Governor in Council, but not to exceed the maximum of one dollar per day.
This is a yearly increase ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Not necessarily. The regulation may provide for a yearly increase or an increase for merit also.

I think the amendment suggested by the Prime Minister to section 3 is an improvement. At the same time. I feel that few persons would be willing to engage in a service of this kind unless they got the ordinary pay that they can get outside for other service. I think $1 per day is a small maximum and might be increased While I am on my feet, if I am in order, I would inquire what is to become of the general ? Will the Minister of Militia explain-
Sir WILFRID LAURIER, We will come to that presently.
Resolution reported and agreed to, and referred to the Committee of the Whole on Bill (No. 5) respecting the Militia of Canada.
House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution :
Resolved, that the director general of ordnance shall be paid at the rate of $3,200 per annum.- Sir Frederick Borden.

I move that the word 1 director ' be struck out and the word ' master ' be inserted instead thereof. This is in accordance with the latest phraseology in the English army. The master general of ordnance will be paid $3,200 per annum, which, I may explain, is his present rate of pay.
What are the duties of this officer ?

To deal with stores of all kind-ammunition, rifles, ordnance, and so on. The inspection of clothing and the issuing of clothing to the force all over the Dominion and the care and issuing of rifles, are under his control.
He is a military officer ?	*

Yes. Until a year ago this department was in the civil branch of the service, and was known as the stores branch. It is now called the ordnance branch, and is placed under the supervision of the general officer commanding. It was formerly directly under the control of the minister.
Who fills the position ?
Colonel Macdonald.
Did not district No. 1 have an officer of this kind at one time, to look after the rifles, armouries, and so on ?
No ; Mr. Dawson, who was in charge of the stores, was an officer of the stores branch. He is now an officer of the ordnance branch. The hon. gentleman is speaking of London ?
Yes. I understood that he was an officer whose duty it was to inspect the various armouries in that district.

That is the district staff adjutant. That is a matter of inspection, which is a different thing from this.
Resolution reported as amended and agreed to, and referred to Committee of the Whole on Bill (No. 5) respecting the Militia of Canada.
House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution,
That the pay and allowances of the officers of the general staff, headquarters staff, and district staff, respectively, not provided for in the Bill respecting the Militfa of Canada, shall be fixed by the Governor in Council.-Sir Frederick Borden.

I do not know whether the Minister of Militia contemplates, under this resolution, to consider the propriety of increasing the pay of the district officers commanding, but it must be within his knowledge that those officers are receiving ' very small remuneration, considering their position and the cost of living in their position. I would like to ask some explanation from the Minister of Militia as to what he intends to do in this matter ?

At present some of the officers of the headquarters staff, the three to whom I have referred, are provided for ; there is power under the present law to provide for others by Order in Council. Several are receiving salaries of $2,400 and I think $2,800. is the highest. As the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) says the district commanding officer's pay as provided for under the present law is altogether inadequate. It has been possible by liberal allowance of various kinds to bring it up to something like what it ought to be, but the pay of the district officer commanding has been only about $1,700 or $1,800. By certain allowances in the way of light, fuel, and so on, some of these officers are now getting about $2,400 or $2,500 but it was thought wiser to leave this matter to the Governor in Council because there are some districts in Canada where the cost of living is much greater than in others. There are some districts too where the work is much greater than in others and therefore it is almost impossible by an Act of parliament, in view of the constant changes that are going on in a growing country like this, to provide properly or justly for new conditions which are bound to arise within the next five or ten years. Therefore it was thought wise to leave this matter to the Governor in Council as is done in the Imperial army, as is done in Australia and I believe almost everywhere else. I may say, in a general way, that, while I am unable to state the amount now, there will undoubtedly be an increase and, I hope, an increase which will be satisfactory to the officers and will bear some proportion at least to the honourable and responsible position which they occupy.	.
Will those three parties named in this section take the position of a general ?

Oh, no, there is still another one coming. [DOT] [DOT]
Resolution reported, read the second time and agreed to, and referred to Committee of the Whole on Bill (No. 5) respecting the Militia of Canada.
House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution :
Resolved, that there may be appointed an officer who shall hofld rank not below that of colonel in the militia, or in His Majesty's regular army, who may be, subject to the regulations and under the direction of the minister, charged with the military inspection of the militia ; and such officer shall be paid at such rate, not exceeding six thousand dollars per annum, as may be prescribed.-Sir Frederick Borden.
Why has the change been made making this permissive instead of obligatory ?

This is an entirely new clause. My hon friend is per-Mr. CLARKE.	*
haps thinking of the clause which provides for the appointment of a general officer commanding. This provides for military inspection corresponding to what exists under the new system which has been adopted in England since I introduced my Bill. The officer would be known as the Inspector General.
I have mistaken the clause.
I will make a very brief explanation because this matter will all be discussed on the second reading of the Bill or in committee.
Who performs the inspection of militia now ?

There is no inspection in this sense at all. I may say that in England since the report of Lord Esher's war office reconstruction committee has been made, the British government, with the approval, I may say, of the whole British peopie have adopted a new system which briefly means that there is to be an army council composed of four leading military men, the secretary of state for war, the deputy minister or rather the under secretary, the accountant general or financial member of the war office, seven men. These compose the army council as it is called. The leading military member of this council is known as the chief of the general staff. He is charged with the duty of advising as to the military policy of the country, and the operations which would be necessary to lit an army for action in the field are under his control The services of the commander in chief at the war office are dispensed with, and there is no longer a commander in chief. There is, however, an important officer, known as the inspector general, whose duty it is to inspect and report to the minister and the army council on the exact condition of things. The inspector general is an independent officer appointed by the government, and he is called upon to report as to the progress which is being- made in carrying out the policy which the army council adopts. I think it is desirable that in this country while we are passing a new militia law, we should make provision in this law to enable us, if we choose, to adopt the system which has just been adopted in England. Therefore, I have introduced this resolution. I have given notice of a similar resolution in reference to an officer to hold the military command, but it would not be intended or expected that in times of peace or under ordinary circumstances both of these officers would be under employment at the same time, and therefore, although there might be an apparent increase in the authority required for the expenditure of money in reality both offices would not he filled at the same time. It would, however, be inconvenient not to have the power. I gave notice on the 18th April-which notice

will be found in the votes and proceedings of that date-of an amendment to the Bill by which the alternative of appointing an officer to command or inspect might be open to us. Upon further consideration I thought it better to introduce two different resolutions because an emergency might arise under which it would be necessary, in the event of a rebellion or any very serious riots, to appoint a general officer commanding although the policy might have been adopted which has been adopted in England of utilizing an inspector general for the pui-pose of inspection. This power under the clause which I proposed would not have then existed, and there would have been no power under which the government could appoint a general officer commanding. Now it is proposed to provide for these two officers, but the understanding is that if the English system be adopted, and I must say that I favour it myself very strongly, there would not be a general officer commanding ordinarily but there would be an inspector general. Under this clause we take power to pay him at a rate not to exceed $6,000 per annum. I may say in this connection that it is my opinion, and I think the whole country will approve of this too, that to fill the important position of inspector general an imperial officer of standing and experience should be appointed.
Are you making provision that he shall be an imperial officer by this clause ?
No, that he may be.	.

Am I to understand from the hon. minister that there is to be no general officer commanding under this new scheme, but that we are to have on a small scale a council of war established, consisting of the hon. the Minister of Militia and Defence and three or four military officers, and also a financial adviser? I understand that it is the intention of the hon. minister to adopt the scheme that has been reported by a commission which had been appointed to investigate the condition of the English war office, but which has not been tried yet. It has only recently come into force. There has been very little experience as to its working as yet. In the meantime is it the intention of the hon. minister that there shall be no general officer commanding, but that power shall be taken to appoint two officers, one an inspector general and another a general officer commanding ?

What I said, and I will repeat it, is that a new system has been adopted in England and we have been in the habit in this country of following the English system. I presume we shall continue to do so as long as we remain a colony of Great Britain. It is very desirable that we should do so, because, if a British army is ever to co-operate with a Canadian
army on Canadian soil, it is exceedingly desirable that the system shall be as near as possible the same in both armies. 1 said it would be undesirable to do anything which would interfere with our power to appoint, a general officer commanding, but I did think it would be a wise thing in view of what has taken place in England and in view of the fact that we are passing a new law which may be supposed to remain in existence for many years to come to. take power to adopt the English system if we think it desirable to do so.
I understood from the hon. minister that the inspector general was to be the head of the military organization except in times of war.	[DOT]
No.
Who is to be the head ?

Well, probably the minister will be the head assisted by the chief of the general staff who will be the chief military adviser of the government. He would more nearly take the place of the general officer commanding than any other officer. The command would then devolve very much more than it does now upon the commanding officers in the different districts. The commanding officers of the different districts to-day are more or less officers who register the views of the officers at Ottawa. They have very little, almost absolutely no power. Provided the scheme were adopted which has been adopted in England very much more power of initiative would be given to the officers of the different districts, but, as I said, this question would require no doubt very considerable discussion and as there are several hon. gentlemen who are not here to-night who would be interested in taking part in it, perhaps it would be better to leave it until the Bill comes up for a second reading. In the meantime no harm can come of this because all I am asking is to take power to make this appointment in case we wish to do so.

I do not offer any opposition to the hon. minister having the power or to having the resolution passed. I am asking for information. Are we to have two officers, one a general officer commanding, and the other an inspector general, or is it the intention that in case of emergency the inspector general shall be the officer commanding and that he shall assume the duties of that position and direct the forces?

No. At the present time we have a general officer commanding. We may continue the general officer commanding. If we continue to have a general officer commanding as we have now we will not take any action under this resolution at all, but if later on it is possible to adopt the English system

then it will he necessary to appoint an inspector general and in that case the general officer commanding would not be necessary.

Of course I have all the difficulties of one who has not very much acquaintance with military matters, but it would seem to me that we may get a little too much machinery in connection with our military affairs if we closely follow the enactments in tha mother country, where they have a very large standing army and where, I suppose, they have a very much larger militia force than we have. They will have under these various officers in the mother country a standing army of 300,000 or 400,000 men and a very large militia force, but do we really require quite so much detail ? Do we require so many boards and such a variety of officers as seem to be contemplated by this statute ? We have at the present time a general officer commanding. Well then this Bill makes provision for some other kind of an officer, and I myself confess that I am a little puzzled as yet to know just why you should call him one thing at one time and call him something else at another time, because, apparently, he has corresponding powers in times of peace with those that the general officer will have in times of war. Is that not the case ?

The Inspector General has nothing to do with policy ; he simply reports carefully on the facts so that the government may know from a qualified officer whether the policy is being efficiently carried out.
The General Officer Commanding has some duties to perform at present, and he is supposed to be of some service to the country. If this change is made who will perform these duties in time of peace ?

The council will act. In England the council is composed of the minister as chairman, the first military officer who is Known as chief of staff, the adjutant general, the quartermaster general, and the master general of ordnance. These military officers are appointed for four years. While it is true that the militia in England far exceeds ours, numerically, and the British army exceeds by 200 times our small permanent force, yet there is no part of the military system so important as to have an efficient staff and to have in that staff all the requisites which might be necessary in the event of the militia being called to take the field. It never can be effective unless it has the machinery at the very heart and centre of it, by which an army can be efficiently operated. Of course we would not need the number of officers they have in England. There the adjutant-general would have under him half a dozen directors-general ; in Canada Sir F. W. BORDEN.
he might only have one or none at all. The quarter-master general in England would have numerous subordinate officers while i'l this country he might only have two, and so also in the case of the master general of ordinance who would have under him a technical director of artillery, and we have that officer now. I may say that the adoption here of the British system, would not I believe increase the expenditure one dollar, although perhaps we might have to provide one additional officer. I would ask my hon. friends who take an interest ir the matter to read this War Office report.
Will you send us copies of it ?
I will send the hon. gentleman a copy with pleasure.
I have read this report, and I think I have a fairly good understanding of the system recently established in Great Britain.
How long has the system been established ?

Just recently. I agree that it is a matter of some doubt as to whether it will be as great an iin-provenment as is hoped for, but if the horn gentleman (Mr. Clarke) reads that report, I think for the time being he will be convinced as I was. I have, however, some little difficulty as to its application to Canada. This inspector general has been called in England, ' the eyes and ears of the army council,' but I do not find anything in the resolution which speaks of the establishment of an army council in Canada.
1 have given notice.
Of course there would be no use of having an inspector gen-eial unless you had an army council.

What does the General Officer Commanding do now ? Does he not go about and inspect the camps, and make reports to the minister as to efficiency and so on ? What duties would be discharged by the inspector general that are not now discharged by the General Officer Commanding ?

The Commander in Chief in England, whose office has been abolished, did the same thing. I fancy the object is to somewhat lessen'the rather too numerous and too onerous duties which rested on the General Officer Commanding.

Who would be the officer commanding in England in case of a crisis ?
Mr. a. T. THOMPSON. In the event of war, one would be appointed. In the meantime. each officer commanding in the eight district into which the British Isles are

divided, is in ms way the general officer commanding in that particular district; while at the same time the inspector general inspects these districts and reports to the army council. For instance, Colonel Otter in Toronto would be the general officer commanding in that district, while the inspector general would rejjort on all the districts. I am not arguing as to whether it would be advisable for us to adopt the army council system or not, but X understand the minister says we can discuss that on the Bill.
Would not that imperial officer in Halifax be in command of the forces here in case of war ?
The new Bill does away with that anomaly, because the officer in Halifax might be the junior of the general officer commanding in Canada.
And if we follow the English system we would have a military council here ?
Quite so. That is the point I elicited. You cannot have an inspector general without a council, because there would be no one to whom the inspector general could report.
The Minister of Militia will be the war Lord ?
Quite so.
What conditions exist in Canada which would make the English system applicable here ?

Our organization has always been an imitation of the organization of the war office, and as they have changed we have changed. They tried for many years to get along with a commander in chief, and in 1890, the Hart-ington Committee which went into the matter very carefully reported against the existing system and recommended very much the same organization as that recommended by the Esher Committee.
Was that owing to its great magnitude ?

No, it was owing to the fact that the Secretary of State for war was responsible to parliament for the condition of the army, but as a matter of fact, he could not be responsible because a great deal of the time he did not know what was going on, as proved to be the case during the Boer War. It was to cure a fatal difficulty of that kind that this 'system was adopted. In a word, the British government has now adopted the system which has been in force in the navy for a century, and which has been found to work admirably*. Germany and the United States have both adopted the same system.

It appears to me that
there is a great deal in what the hon. minister has said in regard to the proposed changed condition of affairs in his department, and I have every confidence that his interest in. and knowledge of his department is such as to effect an improvement upon the past. But it seems to me that there is a great deal of machinery employed that might he saved; for instance, the council consisting of seven, all of whom must be paid.
Not one of them. They are all paid officials now, and there will be no additional expense.
That lessens in part the objection which I had. The inspecting ! officer is an independent officer, but he is subject to the dictation of the council.
No, he is appointed by the council and must report to the council ; but he reports on the cold facts as he finds them.

That I approve of. It appears to me that the general officer commanding should be an imperial officer, one well up in the art and tactics of war, a man who is equal in every respect to the duty he assumes. I think we would place ourselves in a better position by appointing such an officer in general command than we would if we appointed one from the militia who had not seen active service and had never had the smell of powder. I think that should be one of the primary objects in framing the Bill now before the House.
Resolution reported, read the second time and agreed to and referred to Committee of the Whole on Bill (No. 5) respecting the Militia of Canada.
